newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to cut troop strength abroad by 30 percent.
newsitem.headline: France to cut troop strength abroad by 30 percent.

text.p: France will cut the number of its troops serving aboard, apart from those in former Yugoslavia, from 56,000 to 39,000 over the next six years, the army's monthly magazine said in its latest issue.

Terre Magazine said the cuts were part of sweeping reforms which will see overall military strength drop from half a million to 350,000 because conscription will be scrapped by 2002 and replaced by all-professional forces.

The magazine said the only areas outside metropolitan France where units would keep their present organisation intact were the east African state of Djibouti and French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
France has 3,400 troops in Djibouti, wedged on the strategic Red Sea coast, and 3,700 in French Guiana, keeping watch over the launching base for European Ariane space rockets.
Countries where military strength would be reorganised included Germany and the African states of Senegal, the Ivory Coast, Gabon, Chad and the Central African Republic, the magazine said.

Defence Minister Charles Millon said earlier this year that no bases would be abandoned even if the number of troops dropped. His aim was to allay the fears of African leaders who count on French forces to defend their borders or their rule.

The magazine gave no figures for French troop strength for African countries under the plans. But German sources said earlier this year that the number of French troops in their country, which once reached 50,000, would drop to only 3,000.

There would also be reorganisation of units in the French West Indian islands of Martinique and Guadeloupe, the Indian Ocean island of Reunion, and New Caledonia and French Polynesia in the Pacific, the magazine said.

It said there would be an increase in the number of troops sent for four-month training stints to overseas bases and a corresponding drop in the number of personnel assigned there with families for two-year postings.
